summary: The note is a Wikipedia article on the rebound effect (conservation), the reduction in expected gains from efficiency improvements caused by behavioral or systemic responses such as increased consumption. It traces the concept from William Stanley Jevons (1865) through Daniel Khazzoom, Len Brookes and Harry Saunders (the Khazzoom-Brookes postulate), classifies rebound types from super conservation to backfire, and separates direct, indirect and economy-wide effects. It also covers empirical findings on income level variation and time-related rebounds; the text is truncated before its suggested solutions section.
one_line: Wikipedia article on the rebound effect, where efficiency gains lead to increased resource consumption, reducing expected savings.
key_facts: The rebound effect is defined as the reduction in expected gains from new technologies that increase the efficiency of resource use, because of behavioral or other systemic responses.

Thiesen et al. (2008) define the rebound effect as the fact that efficiency improvements often lead to cost reductions that provide the possibility to buy more of the improved product or other products or services.
If a 5% improvement in vehicle fuel efficiency results in only a 2% drop in fuel use, there is a 60% rebound effect.
The note lists five rebound types: super conservation (RE < 0), zero rebound (RE = 0), partial rebound (0 < RE < 1), full rebound (RE = 1), and backfire (RE > 1).
Backfire, where RE is greater than 1, is commonly known as the Jevons paradox.
William Stanley Jevons first described the rebound effect in his 1865 book The Coal Question.
Jevons wrote: "It is a confusion of ideas to suppose that the economical use of fuel is equivalent to diminished consumption. The very contrary is the truth."
Daniel Khazzoom is credited by most contemporary authors for the re-emergence of the rebound effect in the research literature, based on energy efficiency gains in home appliances.
Len Brookes argued in Energy Policy that economically justified energy efficiency improvements would stimulate economic growth and increase total energy use.
In 1992, economist Harry Saunders coined the term Khazzoom-Brookes postulate to describe energy efficiency gains paradoxically resulting in increased energy use.
Recent studies have demonstrated that direct rebound effects are significant (about 30% for energy).
In developed countries, the direct rebound effect in residential space heating and cooling usually ranges from roughly 5% to 40%.
Indirect effects from household conservation can range from 10% to 200% depending on the scenario, with higher indirect rebounds from diet changes aiming to reduce food miles.
Computational general equilibrium (CGE) models indicate economy-wide rebound effects are likely to be very high, with estimates above 100% being rather common.
In a rural India solar lighting case study, direct rebounds were between 50 and 80%, and operating hours for lighting rose from an average of 2 to 6 per day.
